subject: frostAxe
pitch:
Category: Fantasy weapon.
Subject: frost-forged battle axe.
Style: League of Legends.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for a frost-forged battle axe in a League of Legends style—stylized, ornate, glowing icy crystals, bold silhouette, standing on a small staged base. I'm aiming for something substantial but manageable, prioritizing correctness and quality since I can't test it directly.

For the structure, I'll use a root joint at the origin since the builder likely requires at least one joint even for prop-style objects. I'm deciding on orientation: the axe stands vertically with its haft along Y, its butt sunk into an ice-stone plinth base, and the blade's broad face oriented toward +Z so it reads clearly from the front, with the blade extending toward +X and a counter-spike or ice crystal balancing it on -X.

Now I'm planning out proportions and components: roughly 1.55m total height, with a 0.12m frosted stone base holding the embedded haft butt, an octagonal plinth with runes and ice crystal clusters, a vertical haft swept as a rod with dark blue-steel coloring and wrapped leather grip bands plus metal collar fittings and glowing rune inlays, and a pommel capped with an ice crystal spike at the bottom.

I'm now working out the socket collar mounting the blade onto the haft around the 1.15–1.35m mark, and sketching the crescent blade's outline in relative coordinates—plotting the top horn, attachment point, and cutting edge curve so the shape tapers correctly from haft center outward.

I realize the edge arc between the two horns looked concave rather than convex, so I'm adjusting the horn and midpoint x-values to bow the cutting edge outward like a proper bearded axe.

I'll keep smoothing at 1 since the corner-cutting shouldn't cause self-intersection near the sharp horn tip. Now I'm layering the blade body, starting with the dark steel base shape.

Writing paint gradient logic...

Thinking Freljord aesthetic—pale blue, white, bone, bronze trim for contrast against the icy glow. For the blade edge, I'm sweeping a thin glowing white tube along a curved path through the crescent's outer points to create a defined rim.

Then I'm planning icy crystal spikes extending from the horn tips, faceted six-sided shards in pale ice tones with glow but no transparency, and a spiked fluke detail on the back side.

Still designing crystal geometry...

I'll drop the nested translucent idea and instead give crystals vivid cyan hues from a small palette with varying glow strength, since each color/strength combo just needs its own material. I'm also thinking about adding frost shard cards scattered near the socket and base, plus considering fur trim details fitting the Freljord theme.

Writing ring and tuft code...

I'll set up three joints — root at the base, haft parenting the handle, and head parenting the axe head — assigning parts to each so the model reads as a proper rigged hierarchy, then work out the vertical measurements for the plinth top, haft span, and head center.

Now I'm mapping the full vertical layout: spearhead tip around 1.58-1.62, haft top near 1.38, and crystal horns reaching about 1.66, giving an overall height close to 1.65-1.66m. I'm also figuring the footprint radius needed at the base to comfortably support the blade's horizontal spread.

Designing the lathe profile for the stone plinth...

I'm thinking a thin flat ring decal with rune glyphs could sit on the plinth's rim, visible between the snow mound's edge and the outer radius, mapped onto an SVG texture plane facing upward.

Since actual runic unicode glyphs likely won't render in a raster font, I'll draw the runes as simple stroked path shapes instead, defining several glyph-like path strings in small boxes and rotating copies of them around the circle.

Still calculating rune placement radii...

Checking that the rune ring sits just past the flat edge of the lathe profile, I realize the flat top needs to extend slightly further to r=0.35 so the runes don't hover off the edge. Adjusting the lathe profile points accordingly...

Now I'm thinking about adding ice crystal clusters outside the plinth near the floor, around radius 0.45, tilted outward so they don't overlap the carved rune ring—placing a few clusters at opposite corners rather than hanging anything above the mound.

For the haft, I'm defining the core shaft as a straight swept path with a circular faceted cross-section, using a dark steel-blue wood grain texture for a weathered look.

I'm wrapping leather bands around the grip with diagonal stripe patterns in brown and dark leather tones, plus flat end caps, and adding bronze lathe-turned rings at several points along the haft for metal reinforcement detailing.

I'll add a fur collar ring near y=0.9, then design hanging leather cords with bone trinkets and an ice crystal charm dangling off the socket using a curved bezier path. For the head assembly itself, I'm placing the center at [0,1.12,0] and building the socket as a lathed cylinder starting around y=0.88 where the haft passes through.

Writing collar geometry...

I should rename the unused parameter to avoid typecheck issues, and I'm now planning an inner etched crystal inlay for the blade — an elongated diamond/crescent shape with a glowing cyan outline, slightly protruding beyond the blade surface.

For the layered look, I'll add a darker navy snowflake decal plane on top at a slight z-offset, so it reads as crisp etching against the glowing cyan inlay rather than glowing itself — keeping the glow effect isolated to the inlay only, with the snowflake drawn in deep navy plus white highlights for contrast.

I'm also working out the blade geometry — since thickness tapers only along y, I'll rely on a beveled edge (around 0.014) toward the +x side to fake a sharpened look, and I'm adding a bronze trim guard plate near the haft as a separate laminate extrusion over a specific x-range.

Now I'm defining that root plate's outline and dimensions, giving it a 0.05 thickness and bronze coloring, with rivets placed symmetrically on both sides as small gold spheres embedded into the surface at z=±0.025.

I'm adding an icy glow along the blade edge and planning a row of frost crystals growing along the top edge using the path points, deciding to compute crystal positions manually from the polyline rather than relying on a path-following helper.

Then I'm placing crystal spikes at the horn tips — one angled upward near the top, one angled downward near the bottom — giving them a glowing cyan tint to contrast with the steel blade.

For the rear fluke, I'm painting it dark steel using the blade function, then growing a small cluster of backward-pointing crystal spikes from its base at varying angles and sizes. Now I'm starting the top spear socket with a lathed profile for the haft attachment.

Still defining crystal geometry...

I'm planning fur tufts at the collar using a tapered white-blue blade shape, plus small bone-bead and crystal charms on a leather cord. I'm also considering adding a bronze emblem disc with an ice-blue rune on the socket's front face, figuring out placement relative to the octagon collar geometry.

I'll skip the rear gem and keep it simple—settle on five textures total (runes, snowflake, tuft, emblem, frost accents) rather than adding plinth relief or extra decals, and consider small glowing rune-glyph planes along the haft instead.

For the haft layout, I'm working out placement: a glowing rune strip plane positioned around 0.03 wide by 0.12 tall, mounted front and back on bare haft sections between the grip wrap and rings—roughly snow at 0.11–0.17, a bronze ring at 0.24, wrap from 0.26–0.60, another ring at 0.62, the rune strip at 0.66–0.86, and a possible final ring near 0.88.

I'm placing a fur collar at 0.86 just under the socket, with the socket spanning 0.86 to 1.38 to align with the haft top, then a cap and spear tip bringing total height to around 1.7 — tall but acceptable since nothing else needs to hang above it. For hanging charms, I'm positioning a cord attached near the collar bottom that drapes down past the fur, threading beads at y-values 0.82, 0.78, and 0.74, with a small crystal charm pointing downward at 0.70.

Now I'm adding frost and snow accents: painting white snow on upward-facing surfaces where the normal points up and noise exceeds a threshold, giving frosted edges on the blade, socket, and haft tops. I'm also checking that the flat color palette stays under 64 distinct colors and estimating the total part count — aiming for 150–250 by tallying the plinth, mound, runes, rocks, crystal clusters, haft segments, and head details, and considering whether to add extra set pieces like stone pillars or an anvil for a forge theme.

I'm settling on a stone-and-ice plinth base with embedded ice chunks, plus small details like bronze rim studs, squashed snow dollops, and downward-pointing icicles along the rim edge. Writing helper functions...

Checking the normal direction for the horizontal profile segment confirms it faces downward correctly, so the flat bottom cap works as intended. Now I need to handle the `dir` parameter, which could be passed as a vector or array for orientation.

Glow requires a MeshStandardMaterial (or one named "paint"), and I'm setting up the ice crystal palette with four blue-white hex colors. I also need to support a `bone` option that lets parts attach to a specific joint for custom rigging.

Now I'm defining the stone paint function: blending two gray-blue base tones with noise, darkening along cell cracks, and layering a snow tint near the top using a smoothstep threshold on surface normals.

I'm checking the module's exports — noise, cells, mix, smoothstep, paint, resolve, rgb all come from the core builder package, while kits like glow and metal (clockwork) are separate imports, so I'll use metal("bronze"), metal("blued"), metal("steel"), and metal("verdigris") for the material variants.

Instead of a toon kit, I'll go for a League of Legends splash-art feel with hand-painted stylized lighting — writing a custom shading helper that tints colors warm on top and cool underneath based on surface normal direction, blending between a cool violet-blue and a warm tone using smoothstep.

Setting up imports from the builder library and its glow/clockwork kits, defining lightweight local types for color handling instead of importing them directly since I'm not sure what's exported.

Writing the axe's joint hierarchy...

I'm sketching the plinth base using a lathed profile with a stone color and eight segments for a faceted look, then planning bronze studs spaced around the rim at a small radius near the chamfer edge.

Next I'm defining a snow mound shape as another lathed profile with smoother segmentation, finished with a mottled white-blue snow texture.

The haft sinks slightly into the mound at y=0.14. I'm adjusting the rune ring and mound radii to avoid overlap, and planning scattered rocks using flattened icosahedron geometry positioned around the plinth base, textured with a stone paint.

Rotating the icosahedron about y keeps those extremes stable, so I'll settle on a sink depth of about 0.58 times size for the centerpoint. Now I'm planning crystal cluster placement on the floor—positioning a few clusters at varied angles and scales around the scene, like front-left small, back-right large, and left-back, each with its own tilt direction.

Each cluster gets a main crystal tilted outward plus smaller satellites, with the base sunk just slightly below floor level so tilted rims don't clip above the surface—working out the sink math so it stays within about 2% of the crystal height.

Placing four clusters around the plinth at radius ~0.5-0.52: one at 40° (front-left), one at 150° scaled up as the largest back-left feature, one at 235° (back-right), and one at 320° (front-right). Converting angles to x/z coordinates confirms the overall model width stays within bounds and won't collide with the blade extending forward.

Now I'm building the haft shaft as a swept octagonal rod from near the base up to the top, painting it with a dark grained texture, then adding a wrapped band rod partway up the handle using the same sweep approach with flat caps.

For the wrap texture I'm using a stripe pattern of dark browns with some wobble to simulate leather binding, placing one wrap segment mid-haft and considering ring markers at specific heights for added detail. I'm also planning a bare section of the haft for a rune strip, adding thin front and back planes offset slightly in depth to carry inscribed markings.

Now I'm sketching the rune glyph shapes as small SVG paths arranged vertically, aiming for a glowing cyan etched look with simple angular strokes representing three distinct runes.

I'm also working out the front/back plane orientation for the mesh, then planning a fur ring near the top using a frame-based ring placement with tuft cards generated at each point.

Writing the lathe profile for the head socket...

I'm figuring out where to place the bronze decorative bands around the socket, trying to position them so they don't overlap with the emblem plate in the middle.

Checking that the boss emblem sits proud of the root plate without clashing geometrically, then starting to write the blade outline coordinates.

Writing the blade extrude code...

Verifying the bevel stays under half-thickness and that paint coordinates map correctly, then sketching out the edge sweep path with its control points and radius.

Adjusting coordinates...

Now I'm thinking about the edge glow color for the icy blade tint, and designing a smaller crescent inlay shape with its own outline points and smoothing, checking where the inlay boundary sits relative to the blade edge.

I'm checking that the inlay stays within the blade's boundary with enough margin, then adding a snowflake texture overlay with six rotated arms drawn in navy stroke lines.

Writing SVG code...

Since the snowflake is tight against the inlay boundary, I'll shrink the plane width slightly for safety. For the decal placement on both front and back faces of the bone head, the symmetric snowflake design means mirroring from the back view doesn't cause any visual issue.

Now I'm adding the root plate and rivets: extruding the bronze plate, checking its outline clears the socket collar, then placing small gilt-colored rivet spheres at calculated positions along the plate face. I'm also considering adding subtle ice-crack line details within the icy blade zone using cell boundary distances to darken thin cracks.

Then I move to the rear fluke — extruding it with the same blade paint, adding a mirrored bronze cuff plate at the root with its own outline and thickness, and carefully defining the fluke's outline points to curve from the haft out to a tip and back without self-intersecting.

Now I'm placing crystal spikes along the fluke: one at the tip extending outward, a couple more near the top edge at varying angles and lengths, and an icicle hanging from the underside, each with its own direction vector and radius — some wider than the blade itself so they visibly protrude and read as frost growth. I'm also scattering frost crystals along the top edge of the front blade at several points along that curve.

For the horns, I'm adding one crystal growth at the top horn angled forward-up and another at the bottom horn angled forward-down, checking their tip positions don't collide with the model base. Then at the very top of the haft I'm lathing a small cap profile and topping it with a four-sided crystal spear in a pale icy-steel color with a glow effect.

Now I'm adding a hanging cord with a curved catmull path, beaded spheres along it, and a small hexagonal crystal charm dangling near the bottom, shaped like a tapered point attached at its flat base.

I need to attach the cord to the socket more precisely, adjusting the position so it sits just inside the flared socket radius instead of outside it. I'm also considering icicle details under the socket but realizing they'd be hidden by the fur tufts there, so I'll skip them and move those icicle shapes elsewhere along the blade instead.

I'll pick a subset of angles for 6 dollops instead of covering every spot. Skipping floating ice shard cards above the piece—nothing needs to hang there. I'll leave out extra floating snow particles too, keeping the composition simpler.

Still writing emblem SVG...

Still writing tuft shapes... I'm positioning the root at the bottom of the card viewBox so the tip points upward.

For the rock plinth, I want strong rim lighting with a saturated hue to match the LoL style. I'm setting up a seeded RNG function for deterministic randomness, then writing the crystal cluster generator -- placing a base crystal at the center with scaled length and radius tilted outward, plus smaller satellite crystals around it.

Still writing crystal placement logic...

Still writing blade shading logic...

Skipping the plinth etching idea for now. I'm placing a rune ring plane above the plinth using a texture, oriented face-up with the z-axis as normal, and checking that its height clears the plinth's flat top surface.

Now I'm defining a helper coordinate system for the head group using an HY offset so parts like extrusions and floating motes position consistently relative to it, and sketching options for sweep geometry like side count and rod radius for the final charm cord.

Working out rod and ring parameters for the fur and wrap details, using options-object style for color, bone attachment, and side count, plus setting up radial card frames facing outward from the surface.

Now I'm planning the haft as a simple two-point sweep with flat caps, and tallying up the rough part count across plinth, mound, runes, studs, dollops, rocks, clusters, and haft to size the scene before writing it out.

Tallying further additions brings the total near 130 parts, and I'm considering small glowing accent details like engraved groove lines along the blade edge and tiny rune-dot studs tracing the inlay border on both faces.

Working out bronze trim framing...

I'm scrapping the molding idea and instead placing small gilt bronze studs around the inlay's perimeter as decorative accents, keeping the count manageable and checking that their positions still fall on the bronze plate region of the blade. Now I'm finalizing the code and double-checking the lathe offset semantics before writing the final version.

I confirm the outline's origin aligns with the `at` parameter along the axis. I'm defining a custom point type to handle sharp corners in the outline arrays, then writing a shading function that resolves colors based on surface normal and position using a smoothstep gradient.

Placing more rocks and crystal clusters...
